analysis.one_liner: Restores automatic survivor benefits and easier eligibility for widows of coal miners disabled by black lung disease.
analysis.headline: Introduced by three coal-state House Democrats with two cosponsors, the bill was sent to a House subcommittee in March 2009 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 1981 rewrite of the Black Lung Benefits Act, widows and other survivors of coal miners lost two things: miners can no longer qualify through a rule that presumes black lung disease after 15 years of coal mine work, and survivors of miners who were already receiving benefits must file a new claim to keep the money coming. This bill would strike both exceptions, restoring the pre-1981 rules for claims dating back to 1981. It never advanced past a House subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Survivors — mostly widows — of coal miners who died of black lung disease or were receiving benefits for it. They would regain benefits without having to build a new legal case after the miner's death, and miners with long coal mine careers would qualify through a presumption that employers would have to rebut with evidence.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Survivors of coal miners with black lung

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the last sentence of section 411(c)(4) of the Black Lung Benefits Act, which had limited the 'rebuttable presumption' — under which a miner with at least 15 years of coal mine work is presumed to have black lung disease unless the evidence shows otherwise — to claims filed before the 1981 amendments took effect.

It strikes the exception in section 422(l) that requires survivors of miners who were already determined eligible for black lung benefits to file a new claim, refile, or otherwise revalidate the miner's claim, so eligible survivors would again receive benefits automatically.

Both changes apply to claims filed on or after the effective date of the Black Lung Benefits Amendments of 1981, meaning survivors whose claims were narrowed by the 1981 rules over the previous three decades would come back into coverage.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators and their insurers, who fund black lung benefit payments and would face more eligible claims and survivors; costs ultimately flow through the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund financed by a tax on coal, so the coal industry and coal consumers bear it.

drawbacks.text: The bill would reopen coverage for claims dating back to 1981, which could generate a wave of retroactive survivor claims and higher liabilities for the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund and the coal operators and insurers behind it, costs that flow back into the price of coal.

The 15-year presumption makes eligibility easier by shifting the burden of proof to employers in long-career cases; an honest supporter would acknowledge that this admits some claims where the medical evidence of work-caused disease is thin and the employer bears the cost of disproving it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and narrow: widows of miners who worked decades underground would not have to re-litigate a dead man's claim or prove medical causation from scratch. The cost — higher benefit liabilities for coal operators and the trust fund they finance — is also real but falls on a concentrated industry with few claimants. The main design question is the retroactive reach back to 1981, which magnifies cost but also covers the very survivors the 1981 rules cut off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee in March 2009, where it sat with no markup, no vote, and no floor action through the end of the 111th Congress.

narrative.text: Rahall of West Virginia introduced the bill on February 12, 2009, joined by Representatives Boucher and Holden, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
The committee reported no action; on March 23, 2009 the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.
The bill drew only two cosponsors, both House Democrats, and never reached a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators and their insurers, who continued to face survivor claims under the narrower post-1981 rules, and survivors of coal miners, who remained without the benefits this bill would have restored.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators and insurers; survivors got nothing

for.name: Rep. Nick Rahall (D-WV)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 12, 2009 to restore survivor benefits under the Black Lung Benefits Act.

for.name: Reps. Rick Boucher (D-VA) and Tim Holden (D-PA)
for.what_they_did: Joined Rahall in introducing the bill, the bill's only cosponsors besides the sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor / Subcommittee on Workforce Protections
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and, after sending it to the Workforce Protections subcommittee on March 23, 2009, took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report.

sides.party_line_note: Only three coal-state Democrats ever sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and no member or bloc is recorded as opposing it — it simply never came up.

industries.industry: Coal mining operators and their insurers
industries.note: Black lung benefits are paid by coal operators, their insurers, and the federal trust fund financed by a coal excise tax. Restoring the 15-year presumption and automatic survivor benefits would have increased the number of paid claims, so the industry's interest in this bill ran directly against the widows and miners it would have helped.
